newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish rate rise may not attract foreign capital.
newsitem.headline: Polish rate rise may not attract foreign capital.

text.p: Foreign investors are not expected to return to the zloty in large numbers even if Polish interest rates rise because of the risks surrounding fundementals and the pending elections, analysts said on Thursday.
However, higher interest rates, which should boost yields on Polish treasuries, would probably attract some speculative foreign capital into the zloty.

"It seems foreign investors are not very secure on Poland and they will most likely remain restrained until the country's situation clarifies," Bohdan Wyznikiewicz, deputy head of the Institute of Market Economic Research (IBnGR) told Reuters.

The National Bank of Poland said on Wednesday that it would raise the nominal interest rates within weeks to offset additional government spending on flood relief, which would only fuel the country's already booming domestic demand.
Analysts, who said a rise could come at any time, expected the NBP to up rates one or two points from the present 22 and 25 percent for the discount and lombard rates respectively.

Investors are also wary of future fiscal restraint after this September's parliamentary polls, which pits the rulling ex-communists against a so far untested right-wing group clustered around the Solidarity trade union.

"There is uncertainty now because of the elections and that is unavoidable, but investors should see the monetary tightening as positive," said Joseph Karazin, chief economist at Societe Generale in London.

Analysts said a growing current account deficit, which could put Poland on the fast track to a Czech-style currency crisis, would in the longer term put the zloty under downward pressure despite zloty-boosting direct investment inflows.

On Thursday the zloty closed at minus 1.27/1.31 percent from its parity rate against a basket of currencies, down from Wednesday's close at 1.14/1.19 percent as yesterday's brief rally on the central bank rate rise pledge ended nearly as quickly as it started.
The zloty closed at 3.4625/35 per dollar, up from 3.4685/00 on Wednesday and at 1.8905/15 to the mark, down from 1.8815/25.
Analysts said massive, zloty-boosting, foreign entry would not start until after the polls, when the 1998 budget was set, with speculative currency trading dominating until that time.

"One entry point could be after parliamentary elections, if a stable coalition takes power...and another could be when next year's budget is adopted around the end of 1997," said Wojciech Kowalczyk, senior dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.
Analysts said however, that the zloty could make a knee-jerk reaction immediately after interest rates were increased, which would likely spark some inflows of more speculative foreign capital.

"There should be some foreign entry after rates are increased, but many are still wary of Poland following a period of high zloty volatility," said Bogdan Stepkowski, senior dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.

The zloty hit an all-time low of minus 5.7 percent from its parity rate two weeks ago amid large scale foreign withdrawal and speculative sales during the initial stages of a devastating flood crisis, which crippled much of southwestern Poland.

Analysts said the 1998 budget gap, which Finance Minister Marek Belka wants to cut to 1.9 percent of the gross domestic product (GDP) from this year's planned 2.8 percent deficit, was still too loose to tighten the reins on the economy.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the OECD want Poland to slash its budget deficit to no more than 1.5 percent in 1998 and to balance its books by 1999.
But analysts said this type of fiscal restraint required making unpopular budget spending reductions, which should not be expected before the elections.
